scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent ten-item B2 assessment draft for Asteroids: A Question of Risk, Not Panic; human pedagogy approval required.

tabs.title: Applying the Argument
tabs.description: Use the text in new situations.

questions.q: A news report says an asteroid will pass close to Earth. What would the writer want readers to ask first?
choices: How many headlines mention the asteroid?
Does the calculated orbit actually cross Earth's path?
Is the asteroid made entirely of rock?
Which telescope photographed it first?
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph distinguishes a cosmic close approach from a predicted intersection with Earth.

questions.q: Why can a revised impact estimate represent scientific progress rather than confusion?
choices: A later measurement is always lower than an earlier one.
Early calculations are not based on observations.
Scientists have changed what they mean by impact.
New observations can narrow uncertainty in the estimated orbit.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two says additional observations refine the orbit, so changing figures need not mean scientists are guessing.

questions.q: What was the main lesson of the 2024 YR4 example?
choices: A worrying preliminary probability can fall as the evidence improves.
An asteroid discovered late in the year is more dangerous.
Once a risk rises, it usually continues to rise.
Only one observatory should issue an impact estimate.
questions.explanation: The impact probability first rose, then fell to almost zero after further telescope observations.

questions.q: Why does the author limit the conclusions that can be drawn from DART?
choices: The spacecraft did not make contact with Dimorphos.
The experiment was conducted entirely by computer.
A successful orbit change does not cover every kind of dangerous asteroid.
The orbital period of the smaller body became longer.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four distinguishes successful deflection of a test target from a guarantee for all asteroid sizes, structures and warning times.

questions.q: Which problem might a news article cause by quoting a single risk figure without its uncertainty?
choices: Readers may mistake a preliminary estimate for a settled prediction.
Readers may fail to learn how telescopes are constructed.
The number may reveal an asteroid's exact composition.
The asteroid may disappear from the observation database.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two warns that a dramatic isolated number can mislead without information about preliminary estimates and uncertainty.

questions.q: Why is advance warning important if an orbit must be changed?
choices: It makes the asteroid easier to photograph in visible light.
A deflection needs time to alter the future path sufficiently.
It removes the need to consider the asteroid's structure.
Warning ensures all countries agree on one public headline.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four notes that changing an orbit is not instantaneous and warning time is a critical constraint.

questions.q: Why does the writer contrast spectacular film explosions with years of quiet observations?
choices: To argue that space films should become more realistic.
To claim that engineering will never be needed.
To recommend suppressing reports about asteroids.
To emphasize that careful monitoring can matter more than drama.
questions.explanation: The conclusion privileges reliable early observation and cooperation over sensational depictions of a crisis.

questions.q: Two observatories publish different probabilities on consecutive days. What public explanation best fits the text?
choices: The second observatory must have made an error.
The asteroid must have changed its direction overnight.
Each estimate depends on available measurements and stated uncertainty.
The first estimate should be deleted without comment.
questions.explanation: The final paragraphs ask researchers to explain why predictions change as evidence is updated.

questions.q: A student says that any asteroid described as 'near Earth' is about to strike. Which response best reflects the article?
choices: In space, 'near' can describe huge distances; the calculated path matters.
Every near-Earth asteroid is small and therefore harmless.
The word 'near' always gives the exact distance in kilometres.
A near object can only be assessed after an impact.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph explains why the everyday meaning of 'near' exaggerates close approaches.

questions.q: A school wants to prepare a reliable public information poster about asteroid risks. What should it prioritise?
choices: Dramatic images without numbers, to avoid frightening pupils.
Only the highest probability ever reported for a given object.
A promise that modern spacecraft can prevent every impact.
Clear distinctions between known facts, uncertainty and preparation.
questions.explanation: The conclusion emphasizes honest risk communication and cooperation rather than panic or promises of total protection.
